Latest Cake Wallet release notes, version 6.5.3: Zcash on Ledger, BitBox02 Nova on iOS and a faster launch, plus Robinhood Chain, charts and Bitcoin accounts.
Notes for the latest Cake Wallet release are always on this page — link or bookmark it and you'll always land on the newest version. Notes for earlier versions are in the pages below.
Covers v6.5.0 (October 12, 2026), v6.5.2 (October 31, 2026) and v6.5.3 (November 2026).

Zcash on Ledger. Add a Zcash wallet from your Ledger to receive, shield and send ZEC, with every transaction approved on the device. You need version 3.9.2 or later of the Zcash app on your Ledger. Sends come from your shielded balance, so if ZEC arrives at a public address, the home screen shows Unshielded Funds Detected — tap it, then Shield Funds, and approve on your Ledger. Works on Android (Bluetooth or USB) and iPhone and iPad (Bluetooth). See Hardware wallet and Zcash.
 BitBox02 Nova on iPhone and iPad. BitBox now works on iOS over Bluetooth, which means the BitBox02 Nova. When you pair a BitBox, on iOS or Android, Cake Wallet shows a Pairing Code — check that it matches the code on your BitBox, then tap Continue.
 Faster launch. The app opens quicker, and wallets load and switch faster, especially on older phones or if you have many wallets.
 Robinhood Chain. Create Robinhood Chain wallets to send, receive and hold ETH and tokens on Robinhood's Ethereum Layer-2. The USDG and USDe stablecoins are shown by default, and a list of tokenized stocks and ETFs can be turned on from the token list. See Robinhood Chain.
 Price charts. A new Charts tab tracks the prices of the assets you choose to follow, with ranges from one hour to all time. Pin a favorite, sort by market cap, gains or losses, and jump straight to buying, selling or swapping. See Charts.
 Bitcoin accounts. Split one Bitcoin wallet into several accounts — separate pockets with their own balance, addresses and history, all backed up by the same recovery phrase. Turn them on under Settings → Bitcoin Settings → Accounts (Onchain). Accounts you no longer use can be archived, on Monero too. See Bitcoin.
 Faster Bitcoin sync. Bitcoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin wallets are ready sooner: your balance is up to date quickly, while older transaction details finish loading in the background.
 Reorganized settings. Every wallet now has its own settings page named after its coin — for example Bitcoin Settings or Monero Settings — holding Nodes, Accounts, Coin Control, Silent Payments, MWEB, Lightning Username and WalletConnect. The wallet section of Settings is now titled with your wallet's name.
 Zano is being phased out. New Zano wallets can no longer be created or restored. Existing Zano wallets keep working for now — back up your seed from Recovery & Keys and consider moving your funds to another Zano wallet. See Zano.

BTC Map. Find places to spend sats near you: BTC Map is now under Featured Apps in the Apps tab and opens btcmap.org in your browser.
 Ready for Zcash NU7. Cake Wallet's Zcash support is updated for the upcoming NU7 network upgrade, so your sends and shielding keep working through it.
 Stronger 2FA. If Cake 2FA is required to access your wallet, the Verify with Cake 2FA step that follows your PIN can no longer be skipped with the back button or back gesture.
 Safer backup restores. Restoring from a backup file now rejects malformed files that try to write outside Cake Wallet's own storage.
 No more wallets stuck on Connecting. Bitcoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin wallets now retry after a failed connection instead of waiting forever, switching nodes or turning Tor on or off takes effect right away, and slow connections time out instead of hanging.
 Zcash: funds at your transparent addresses are now shielded automatically once they add up to more than 0.0003 ZEC (it was 0.005 ZEC).
 Bitcoin and Litecoin: new addresses now use the next unused index, so a gap can no longer leave addresses that a restore doesn't find. Wallets restored with the Electrum seed format no longer reopen with the wrong addresses or balance.
 Bump fee now checks that the replacement transaction matches the original before it's sent.
 While your transaction is being built, the confirmation screen shows Generating transaction... instead of incomplete details.
 Buy and sell: MoonPay now supports Arbitrum, Cash App is now shown as Cash App Pay, and MoonPay and Onramper checkout pages load correctly on IPv6 networks.
 Charts: prices use your locale's thousands separators and a font with evenly spaced digits.
 Restoring from a QR code for a coin this version of the app doesn't support now says This wallet cannot be used in this app.
 Swaps: scanning a receive-address QR code that includes a chain ID (such as ethereum:0x…@1) now fills in the correct address.
 Deleting a Monero wallet no longer leaves a broken entry behind.
 WalletConnect: Solana requests to sign several transactions at once now work.
 Address book: Bitcoin and Litecoin wallets now show up in the wallet picker in every language, and swap refund addresses are never offered.
 macOS: Cake Wallet now needs macOS 13 (Ventura) or later.
 Lightning: the exported Lightning log now includes timestamps, which helps support.

Require PIN after is enforced on resume. When you come back to Cake Wallet after the timeout you set, it now always asks for your PIN, including right after creating or restoring a wallet.
 Links open in your browser. Links to websites, block explorers and release notes now open in your browser instead of inside Cake Wallet, so the PIN lock shows when you come back.
 iOS: if you set up an iPhone from an iCloud backup, Cake Wallet now explains that iCloud doesn't carry over your wallets' passwords (your funds are safe on-chain) and offers to remove those wallets so you can add them again with their recovery phrases. If your saved PIN can't be read, it now tells you to close and reopen the app.
 Charts: very low prices, such as SHIB's, now show their meaningful decimals instead of 0.00, and a crash with some tokens is fixed.
 SwapTrade: only pairs SwapTrade supports are offered, errors are clearer, and refunds show in the trade details.
 When another wallet picks a Bitcoin wallet from the address book, it now gets an on-chain address even while that wallet is on its Lightning or Silent Payments page.
 Refreshed light theme colors.
 macOS: the Cake Pay tile now opens cakepay.com, and the Cake Pay terms link is updated.
 Fixed the bottom bar highlighting the wrong tab when some tabs are hidden, a card customization crash, and sharing on iPad.

Archive accounts. Accounts can't be deleted, but you can now archive the ones you no longer use: open the account's Edit Account screen from the Accounts page and tap Archive Account. Funds stay in an archived account, and you can bring it back any time from Archived Accounts. A short walkthrough explains how accounts work the first time you open them. Works for Bitcoin and Monero accounts.
 More Cake Wallet Tor nodes. Bitcoin and Litecoin now have a Cake Wallet (Tor) onion node in their node lists, and the Monero and Zcash onion nodes moved to new addresses under the same name. With built-in Tor on, Bitcoin fee estimates also come from Cake's own onion service. If you had the old Monero Cake Wallet (Onion) node or an old Zcash Tor node selected, select Cake Wallet (Tor) again after updating.
 Monero core update. Monero is updated to v0.18.5.3.
 Safer Monero sends. A Monero payment that would have to be split into several transactions is now stopped with an explanation instead of being sent as many. Send a smaller amount to yourself first to consolidate your funds, then try again.
 Lightning amounts in sats. Lightning invoice amounts are now entered in sats. The Enable Lightning toggle also no longer disappears after you turn Lightning off, so you can turn it back on later.
 Rescan now fills in your wallet's saved restore height for Monero and Zcash.
 Bitcoin, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin: wallets with many addresses open faster, and your balance no longer briefly shows an old value after sending or receiving.
 Swaps: LetsExchange and StealthEX are no longer offered as swap providers, and Exolix remains off. Past trades with them still show their status in History. In the Swap Tor only mode, Cake Wallet now reaches Trocador through Trocador's onion service.
 Fixed tapping Swap repeatedly creating duplicate trades.
 Buy and sell: MoonPay now offers the payment methods available for your currency, including Cash App and MoonPay Balance, and the confirmation screen shows the provider's minimum and maximum limits.
 Tron: token approvals and other contract interactions no longer show up as token transfers in History, and a slow or failed history lookup no longer stops your wallet from syncing.
 Fixed a send you had backed out of being able to replace a newer one on the confirmation screen.
 BitBox: you're no longer asked to reconnect your device before every send while it stays plugged in.
 When sending or swapping, the wallet switcher now lists only wallets on the same chain.
 Litecoin: coin control's block-explorer link now opens Blockchair.
 iOS: error reports can now be sent through the share sheet when no Mail account is set up.
 Viewing your recovery phrase as a QR code no longer forces the screen to maximum brightness.
 Fixed the History Filters and Support headers rendering in red, and the progress message after deleting a wallet.

Cake Wallet 6.4 release notes: rebuilt buy and sell, redesigned recovery phrase backup, AnyPay redesign, native Bitcoin on Trezor, Solana NFTs, Zcash Ironwood.
Covers v6.4.0 (July 27, 2026), v6.4.1 (August 2026), v6.4.2 (August 27, 2026), v6.4.3 (August 29, 2026), v6.4.4 (September 4, 2026), v6.4.5 (September 20, 2026), and v6.4.6 (October 5, 2026).

Rebuilt buy and sell. Buying and selling now starts from a single Buy or Sell screen with preset amounts, and the fiat currency picker has been reworked — currencies are listed with their country flags, split into Selected, Popular and All Currencies, and searchable. Cake Wallet remembers the currency you picked, and hides the picker entirely on wallets that only support one.
 Clearer wallet backup. What the app used to call your "seed" is now consistently called your recovery phrase, and the screens around it have been redesigned: before anything is revealed you tick three statements confirming you understand what the phrase is, that you will store it safely, and that you will never share it. Wallets that hold a balance are reminded to back up. See Create new wallet.
 AnyPay redesign. Paying a scanned QR code, pasted address, or payment link now walks you through picking the right network: Cake Wallet detects when a recipient address exists on more than one chain, lets you choose the recipient's network, and offers to switch to a matching wallet or swap your current funds to cover the payment.
 Zcash Ironwood network upgrade. Zcash wallets support the Ironwood network upgrade, keeping them compatible with the current network, and the migration is visible in the app: a new "Zcash Network Upgrade" notice explains the migration the first time your wallet starts one, and your balance reads migrating to Ironwood instead of Confirming while it runs. See the Ironwood migration guide for what to expect.
 First round of screen-reader accessibility improvements. With VoiceOver or TalkBack enabled, the swipe-to-confirm control now appears as a regular labeled button — making sending, bridging, and WalletConnect approvals usable with a screen reader — and buttons, input fields, pickers, and the dashboard now announce proper names, values, and states.
 Trezor passphrase for Monero. Monero wallets via Trezor now have full passphrase support.
 Native Bitcoin for Trezor. Pair your Trezor and sign Bitcoin transactions right in the app over USB or Bluetooth — your keys never leave the device. See Hardware wallet.
 Send Solana NFTs. Your Solana NFTs show up in the app's NFTs tab and can now be sent; imported NFTs stay saved, and each NFT shows at a glance whether your wallet still holds it. See Solana.

New buy and sell flow. Buy and Sell now open a single chooser, then a screen with preset amounts (or a custom one). The fiat currency picker shows each currency with its country flag, groups them into Selected, Popular and All Currencies, and can be searched. Your choice is remembered, and the picker is hidden on wallets that only support a single currency.
 Redesigned backup and verification screens. "Seed" is now "recovery phrase" throughout: Settings → Wallet settings → Recovery & Keys, a Recovery Phrase tab, Verify Phrase, and Recovery Phrase or Keys when restoring. Before your phrase is shown you must tick three acknowledgements, and a wallet that holds a balance is reminded to back up.
 Ledger and Trezor over Bluetooth. Both devices can now connect wirelessly, and hardware-wallet operations are thread-safe, so overlapping requests no longer collide.
 Trezor passphrase on the device. You can type a Trezor passphrase on the device itself while pairing, instead of entering it in the app.
 Turning the history toggle off under Settings → Connections now actually stops the block-explorer history calls.
 Cleaner home screen top bar: your wallet name now sits in the top bar next to the coin icon, and Monero accounts are reachable from Settings → Wallet settings → Accounts.
 Message signing and verification now works correctly on Ethereum and other EVM wallets.
 Transaction amounts are calculated with exact integer math, with extra guards against zero or invalid values.
 A Monero wallet that fails to open now reports the error instead of silently doing nothing.
 Transaction notes are included in the history CSV export.
 Transactions at the top of the history list are tappable again, instead of being blocked by the fade overlay.
 Language detection recognises more locales, including Yoruba, Hausa and Guaraní, and Brazilian number formatting is handled correctly.
 Arbitrum wallets use a new default node.
 Updated German translations.
 Fixed spacing in the in-app changelog view.

Native Bitcoin for Trezor. Bitcoin on Trezor now signs natively inside Cake Wallet: pair your device over USB or Bluetooth, enter your PIN if asked, and sign sends right in the app — no Trezor suite, bridge, or separate app needed. Monero on Trezor is unchanged.
 Solana and NFTs improvements. Send your Solana NFTs from the NFTs tab, keep imported NFTs saved across app restarts, and see at a glance which NFTs your wallet still holds (View only marks the ones it no longer holds). When the recipient has never held that NFT's token, the send screen shows the small extra amount of SOL needed to create their token account.
 Swaps.xyz disabled. Swaps.xyz is turned off as a swap provider and no longer appears in the provider picker. Past and in-flight Swaps.xyz swaps stay in your History with their Trade ID — contact Cake Wallet support for any issue with one.
 Monero sync improvements. Sync progress keeps updating while your wallet warms up, so it no longer looks frozen right after opening the wallet.
 A custom node entered under Advanced Settings while creating/restoring a wallet is now connected to right away, instead of starting on the built-in nodes.
 Fixed the contact list going out of sync with your wallets' saved addresses.
 Cake Pay: a stale sign-in session is cleared properly, so Cake Pay asks you to sign in again instead of failing in the background.
 Bitcoin: PSBT handling improved for hardware-wallet sends (change-output derivation info reaches the signing device), and PSBT v0 fallback locktime is parsed correctly.

Zano hard-fork compatibility. Zano wallets are updated for the Zano network's hard fork and keep working with the upgraded network — no action needed on your side.
 Zano now uses standard BIP39 seeds. Newly created Zano wallets get a 12- or 24-word BIP39 seed like your other currencies, can join a wallet group to share one seed across wallets, and support an optional seed passphrase. Restoring accepts a BIP39 seed or the original 26-word native Zano seed, and Zano restores can now use a restore height or date. Existing Zano wallets are unchanged.

Decred now uses standard BIP39 seeds. Newly created Decred wallets get a 12- or 24-word BIP39 seed like your other currencies, can join a wallet group to share one seed across wallets, and support an optional seed passphrase. Restoring accepts a BIP39 seed or the original 15-word native Decred seed. Existing Decred wallets are unchanged.
 Bitcoin sends pick their inputs more privately: Cake Wallet now prefers an exact-match coin set that produces no change output at all, and when some selection freedom exists, chooses coins at random instead of a predictable order.
 Bitcoin transactions set their locktime to the current chain tip (anti-fee-sniping protection), so a miner can't confirm a stale version of your spend in a block from just before it.
 WalletConnect sessions now stay with the wallet that approved them: switching wallets inside Cake Wallet no longer hands a connected dApp session to the new wallet.
 Watch-only Bitcoin wallets no longer show options that cannot work without a private key — Payjoin, Lightning, and Sign & verify are hidden — and Litecoin hardware wallets no longer show the MWEB toggle.
 AnyPay detection and routing reworked under the hood for more reliable multi-network payments.
 Solana: Jupiter swap transactions no longer appear as duplicates or get stuck as pending, token amounts with certain decimal settings parse correctly, and transaction signatures and token mints are now verified.
 Restoring an EVM wallet (Ethereum, Polygon, Base, Arbitrum, BNB Smart Chain) from a mistyped seed now stops with an error instead of creating a wallet you didn't ask for.
 Bitcoin fee estimates coming from Electrum servers are sanitized, so a bad server response can no longer produce an absurd fee.
 You can now send Bitcoin when your wallet's node is reachable on your LAN only, even without internet access.
 The selected transaction speed is now remembered correctly per wallet: Zcash no longer shares Decred's setting, and Dogecoin's choice persists.
 Fixed amounts rendering in scientific notation (like 1.0E-5) and trailing zeros cluttering displayed amounts.
 Fixed scrolling inside the transaction-history sheet.
 iOS: the keyboard now dismisses after restoring a wallet from a backup file.
 Zcash and hardware-wallet connection stability fixes (concurrent Zcash actions, Bluetooth state on the connection screen).
 Further screen-reader improvements: images now announce properly, icon-only buttons are labeled, and addresses are fully read out.
 Light theme fixes: card customizer icons and unchecked checkboxes are now visible.
 Updated German translations.

Zcash: transaction history now shows the real recipient address on outgoing transactions, and no longer shows a bogus one on incoming transactions.
 Zcash: unspendable dust is no longer counted in your Confirming balance.
 Zcash: the address-rotation notice no longer appears on address types that are static, such as Public (Static & Transparent).
 Zcash: fixed the receive address given to swap providers so swaps into ZEC arrive correctly, rescan is more reliable and reports failures instead of stalling silently, and restoring from keys now respects the restore height you enter.
 Zcash: fixed transaction sorting and the fee shown on outgoing transactions.
 Added TBB (The Bitcoin Bull) to the Solana token list — enable it from your Solana wallet's token list.
 Solana tokens verified on Jupiter are now marked as verified and no longer trigger the unrecognized-token warnings.
 Bitcoin wallets now show their master fingerprint under Settings → Wallet settings → Seed & Keys → Keys.
 Restoring from seed now stops with an error if the two passphrase fields don't match, instead of quietly restoring a different wallet.
 Long passphrases now wrap on the Seed & Keys screen instead of being cut off.
 Trezor: fixed an occasional firmware error, and devices now reconnect automatically — including when you back out partway through a flow.
 ENS names that use a custom resolver now resolve correctly.
 Fixed home-screen quick actions when the app wasn't already running.
 The in-app changelog's View more info button now opens these release notes.
 Updated German translations.

Fixed an error that could stop a ChangeNow swap from being created.
 Exolix is temporarily disabled as a swap provider.
 Fixed address lookup for Bitcoin.
 The Yat and Zcash.me toggles under Settings → Connection and sync → Domain lookups now take effect.
 Corrected in-app support links: SwapTrade issues now open the SwapTrade help center, and the Telegram entry label matches where it sends you.
 Updated the in-app text describing where to find your seed and keys (Settings → Wallet settings → Seed & Keys).
 Zcash backend update and other stability fixes.
 Hardware wallet and Bitcoin Cash sends now shuffle the change output properly instead of always placing it last, removing an on-chain fingerprint that could identify Cake Wallet transactions.

Cake Wallet 6.3 release notes: home-screen transaction history, faster Zcash sync, quicker alias sends, Tron swaps via Chainflip, Bitcoin privacy, and Radar.
Covers v6.3.0 (July 21, 2026) and v6.3.2 (July 24, 2026).

Improve how we display recent transactions, limiting it to three on the home screen with the rest of your transactions a tap away.
 Zcash syncing is faster and more stable, and the integration now tracks current network standards.
 Sending to an alias (OpenAlias, ENS, Unstoppable Domains, Yat, Zcash.me and others) resolves more quickly and reliably.
 Swap TRX and USDT on Tron through Chainflip.
 Bitcoin sends now shuffle input order, and payjoin receiving avoids two known fingerprinting patterns, so your transactions blend in better on-chain.
 Radar — Cake's private messaging app with built-in self-custodial Bitcoin Lightning payments — is now available directly from the Apps screen.

Amounts are handled with exact precision throughout the app, fixing rounding and decimal edge cases when typing, converting, or displaying values.
 Upgraded the underlying Flutter engine and completed the next phase of internal refactoring, making the app noticeably more responsive.
 Solana wallets sync and load faster; spam-token detection is stricter on Solana and EVM chains.
 Cake Pay gift card buying is smoother, and all card variants are now shown.
 Lightning improvements: payment preimage in transaction details, better handling when a balance fetch fails, and invoice generation restricted to Bitcoin wallets.
 Receive page: Solana and Tron token info is now included in the QR code and payment link, plus fixes to the copy button and the address rotation control.
 Renaming a wallet is more reliable.
 Hardware wallet fixes for Ledger and Trezor, including a Monero passphrase prompt and correct handling of external outputs on Trezor.
 Added a recovery screen if the wallet database fails to open.
 Silent Payments no longer appear in non-Bitcoin wallets, the tokens button no longer appears on Litecoin, and coin control can no longer be edited from Settings.
 Transaction history layout, month and date localization, desktop QR sizing, and haptic feedback when copying.
 Retired unavailable swap providers, updated the price data endpoint, and hardened the vulnerability disclosure policy.
 Assorted UI polish, dependency bumps, and stability fixes.

Hardware wallets: added a back button to the connect screen, so you can always leave the reconnect flow instead of getting stuck.
 Swaps: your coin control selection is no longer reset when you start a swap, and the paste button on the swap page works again.
 Zcash: addresses are no longer unnecessarily persisted in wallet metadata, and the wallet migration path was corrected.
 Fixed a typo in the multichain receive info box.

Cake Wallet 6.2 release notes: Trezor support for Monero, redesigned WalletConnect, a rebuilt Nodes screen, faster Bitcoin and Litecoin sync, and LetsExchange.
Covers v6.2.0 (June 5, 2026) and v6.2.1 (June 9, 2026).

Use a Trezor hardware wallet with Monero: pair your device to view balances and sign XMR transactions while your private keys stay offline.
 Redesigned WalletConnect screens, with clearer permission prompts, faster session setup, and smoother multi-chain dApp connections.
 Rebuilt Nodes screen: check node latency, switch between your own and Cake's default daemons, and manage your connections in one place.
 Bitcoin and Litecoin wallets sync faster in the background, so the app is ready to use sooner after you open it.
 Smoother Pay Anything flow for scanning, converting, and paying a crypto invoice.

Ongoing code modernization means a smaller app footprint and better memory use.
 General maintenance, performance tuning, and fixes for edge-case UI glitches.

LetsExchange is now re-enabled as a swap provider after extensive improvements to their infrastructure, giving you another excellent source of rates when exchanging coins.
 Fixed a Monero issue where an invalid key image could cause transaction creation to fail.
 Further Trezor improvements.
 QR scan screen fixes: the manual-input button works again, the layout no longer overlaps, and Lightning invoices are parsed more reliably when scanned.
 Solana: the GMT token now displays with the correct number of decimals.
 The swap confirmation sheet now shows the network badge, address book entries show the right chain icons, and the missing MWEB icon is back.
 Sharing now works correctly on iPad.
 Fixed an error when entering an invalid custom node address, and a fix for EVM wallet creation failing after restoring from a backup.

Cake Wallet 6.1 release notes: bridge USDT between Ethereum, Polygon, and Arbitrum in the app, faster navigation, background multi-chain sync, and bug fixes.
Covers v6.1.0 (April 16, 2026) and v6.1.2 (April 23, 2026).

Bridge USDT between Ethereum, Polygon, and Arbitrum directly inside the app, without using an external bridge.
 Faster app: navigation is smoother and asset screens load more quickly.
 Multi-chain wallets stay in sync in the background, so balances and transaction history are consistent across networks.

Fixed issues with Lightning invoice generation.
 Fixed EVM connectivity problems.
 Assorted bug fixes and stability work following the 6.0 launch.

Monero swaps now show up correctly in transaction history, and Monero transaction details show the correct address.
 Bridge screen polish: the keyboard opens automatically, the amount field no longer resizes or gets cut off, and wording on the bridge details and info sheets was corrected.
 Fixed the swap screen not remembering whether fixed rate was turned on or off.
 Pay Anything no longer inserts a token contract address as the recipient, and now automatically selects the token specified in a scanned payment URI.
 Fixed the receive address used for payjoin transactions.
 Clearer descriptions on the wallet restore options.
 Stability fix for Monero wallets to prevent a rare hang while refreshing the dashboard.

Cake Wallet 6.0 release notes: a full app redesign and the Bitcoin Lightning launch, with Lightning addresses, sats display, and a separate unconfirmed balance.
Covers v6.0.0 (February 25, 2026) through v6.0.3 (March 21, 2026). Read more on the blog: Lightning is (finally) here and Our Lightning Journey.

Cake Wallet has been completely redesigned: new home screen, send, receive, swap and settings screens, plus a customizable balance card so you choose which assets and totals appear up front.
 Bitcoin Lightning has arrived. Send and receive Bitcoin in seconds with low fees, built on the Spark Layer 2 via the Breez SDK, and move funds between your on-chain Bitcoin and Lightning balances inside the same wallet.
 Claim your own Lightning address so people can pay you without you generating an invoice first.
 View your Bitcoin balances and amounts in sats instead of BTC.
 Unconfirmed balance is now shown separately on the home screen, so you can see funds that are still confirming.
 Estimated fees are clearer across chains: Solana, Tron, Ethereum and Base now show readable amounts instead of scientific notation.

More accurate sync ETA, and node switching now prefers healthy, unused nodes.
 Pay Anything: better detection of EVM addresses and payment links when you paste or scan.
 Zcash: address detection in the send flow, remembered fee priority, and a Zcash-specific balance card option.
 Monero: customize each account from the new account picker.
 Litecoin MWEB and coin control rebuilt for the new design, including MWEB toggles on the send page.
 Haptic feedback, pull-to-refresh and keyboard handling refined throughout the app.
 Hardware wallets: send amount handling fixed, and Lightning is hidden where it does not apply.

Lightning polish: fee estimation and recipient handling fixed, Lightning addresses load faster, and Cake Pay orders can now be paid over Bitcoin Lightning.
 Turn Lightning support on or off from Settings.
 New in-app changelog screen shows what changed after you update, and Settings gains an About page.
 Swap improvements, a clear "Transaction sent!" confirmation on the swap sheet, and fixes for switching wallets mid-swap.
 Export Lightning and Payjoin logs from Settings so support can diagnose payment issues.
 Copy a receive URI that already includes the amount, straight from the Receive screen.
 Litecoin MWEB balance is no longer counted twice, and enabling MWEB coins works again.
 Solana: send-all fixed, and pasting a Solana address no longer wrongly starts the Pay Anything flow.
 Fixed WalletConnect in the redesigned app, plus fixes to rescan, the node form, address rotation, and keyboard behavior.
 Translation fixes for Spanish, French, German and Dutch, plus a broad translation refresh.

Redesigned Settings, and transaction history filters are back in the new interface.
 Noticeably faster app: smoother transaction list scrolling, quicker receive QR rendering, and faster screen loads.
 More swap pairs on Chainflip: wBTC on Ethereum and USDT on Solana and Arbitrum, plus fixes for USDC and ETH on Arbitrum.
 Hardware wallet QR scanning now accepts BC-UR animated QR codes.
 Better large-screen support, including layout fixes for iPad windowed and split-screen mode.
 Bitcoin transactions now use the standard replace-by-fee sequence value, so fee bumping behaves as expected.
 Lightning: fiat amount calculation on send fixed, and Blink payments fall back to direct broadcast if the first attempt fails.
 Swap fixes for external sends, "send all" with fiat entry, and deposit address switching.

Swaps.xyz and StealthEX are currently disabled as swap providers; all other providers are unaffected.
 Complete Brazilian Portuguese translation.
 Lightning and Payjoin log export are enabled again in release builds.
 Lightning updated to the latest Breez SDK, plus assorted swap fixes.
 Fixed OpenCryptoPay payment requests in the send flow, and switching receive options after generating a Lightning invoice.
 New wallets are now reliably saved immediately after creation, plus minor UI and layout fixes.

How to install Cake Wallet on Android, iOS, macOS, or Linux, then create a new wallet or restore one from a seed phrase, keys, or a backup file.
Cake Wallet is a free, open-source, non-custodial wallet for Monero, Bitcoin, and dozens of other cryptocurrencies. Install it below, then create a new wallet or restore one you already have.

Cake Wallet is available on Android, iOS, macOS, and Linux.

First-time Cake Wallet setup: set a 4- or 6-digit PIN, then create a new wallet or restore one from a recovery phrase, keys, backup file, or hardware wallet.
The first time you open Cake Wallet, it walks you through two quick steps: setting a PIN, and creating (or restoring) your first wallet. The whole thing takes about two minutes.
Open Cake Wallet and tap Set a PIN. By continuing, you agree to the Terms of Service linked on this screen.

Enter a PIN, then enter it again to confirm. Cake Wallet uses a 4-digit PIN by default — tap Switch to 6-digit PIN if you'd like a longer one.
Your PIN protects access to the app on this device. It is not a backup — only your recovery phrase can recover your wallet on another device.

After your PIN is set, choose how to get your first wallet:
Create New Wallet — start fresh. Continue with the Create new wallet guide.
 Restore Wallet — bring an existing wallet into Cake using its recovery phrase or keys, a backup file, a hardware wallet, or the Cupcake app.
If you run into any trouble, contact us using the in-app chat under Support, by email at , or on Telegram.
How to restore an existing wallet in Cake Wallet from a recovery phrase or keys, a backup file, a hardware wallet, a QR code, or the Cupcake app.
Open the wallets menu from the bottom navigation bar, then tap Restore Wallet near the bottom of the screen.

Pick how you'd like to restore, then follow the matching guide:
Recovery phrase or keys — restore from a recovery phrase or the private keys you saved.
 Cupcake — link with our companion air-gapped app installed on a second phone.
 Hardware wallet — connect a hardware wallet device from a variety of manufacturers.
 QR code — restore an air-gapped cold wallet or recover a paper wallet.
 Backup file — restore from a Cake Wallet backup file (available on new installs).

How to restore a wallet in Cake Wallet from a recovery phrase or private keys, choose the Monero seed type, and set a restore height or date for faster sync.
NEVER share your recovery phrase or keys with anyone! If you do, they can steal your funds. Always save them in a safe place!

After tapping Recovery Phrase or Keys on the Restore Wallet screen, choose the currency you want to restore.
Many currencies can be restored from either a recovery phrase or your private keys — you'll switch between the Recovery Phrase and Keys tabs on the next screen. Some currencies support recovery-phrase restore only.

chunks.s: Enter your recovery phrase or keys
chunks.x:
Give the wallet a name, then paste or type in your recovery phrase. To restore from your keys instead, tap the Keys tab at the top and enter them there.
For Monero, make sure the seed type matches your recovery phrase. Tap the seed-type selector and choose Polyseed (16 words), Legacy (25 words), or BIP39 (12 words) accordingly.

For coins that scan the blockchain (such as Monero), set a restore point so Cake Wallet doesn't have to scan the entire chain. Enter the block height from when you first created the wallet, or tap Restore from date and pick a date.
If you don't know the block height, choose a date a few days before you created the wallet. For example, if you created your wallet in February 2020, use January 31st, 2020.
The earlier the date or height, the longer the initial sync takes. Picking a point close to when you first used the wallet keeps syncing fast without missing any transactions.

Tap Restore, then leave your phone awake with Cake Wallet open while it synchronizes. Sync progress is shown at the top of the home screen; once it finishes, your full balance and transaction history will be visible.

Connect a Ledger, Trezor, BitBox, COLDCARD, or Cupcake hardware wallet to Cake Wallet, with supported coins per device and Bluetooth, USB, or QR steps.
Hardware wallet support is limited to specific devices and currencies. Check the lists below before you start.

Connected over Bluetooth or USB
Ledger — Monero, Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, Polygon, Zcash
 Trezor — Monero, Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, Polygon
 BitBox — Bitcoin, Ethereum, Polygon (Android over USB; iPhone and iPad over Bluetooth with a BitBox02 Nova)
Air-gapped, over QR codes — these devices are never plugged in or paired. Cake Wallet displays a QR code, you scan it with the device, and then scan the signed result back into Cake Wallet.
COLDCARD — Bitcoin, using either the BCUR or BBQR QR code format
 Cupcake — Cake's own air-gapped signing app; see the Cupcake documentation
SeedSigner, Keystone and Foundation Passport aren't supported yet. BitBox works on Android, iPhone and iPad only, not on macOS or Linux, and Zcash, including Zcash on Ledger, isn't available on macOS or Linux.
Trezor: Cake Wallet recognizes the Trezor Model One, Model T, Safe 3, Safe 5 and Safe 7. How it talks to your Trezor depends on the coin:

Bitcoin and Monero use Cake Wallet's built-in Trezor connection: select your Trezor in Cake Wallet and approve on the device — no Trezor Suite, bridge, or separate app needed. The Safe 7 connects over Bluetooth or USB; the Model One, Model T, Safe 3 and Safe 5 connect over USB only, and Cake Wallet offers USB on Android only. On iPhone and iPad, that means you need a Safe 7.
 Litecoin, Ethereum and Polygon use Trezor Connect. Cake Wallet skips its own device connection step and opens Trezor Connect outside the app, which passes the result back to Cake Wallet.
Go to the Wallets tab in the bottom navigation bar, then tap Restore Wallet.
On the Restore Wallet screen, tap Hardware wallet, then choose the wallet type.

Connect your hardware wallet device.
On Android, Ledger and Trezor devices can connect over Bluetooth or USB, and BitBox connects over USB. USB connections are available on Android only. On iOS and macOS, Ledger devices connect over Bluetooth. On iPhone and iPad, a Trezor needs to be a Safe 7 (see the Trezor note above), and a BitBox needs to be a BitBox02 Nova, which connects over Bluetooth.
Air-gapped devices such as COLDCARD and Cupcake are never connected: instead of this step, you scan QR codes back and forth between Cake Wallet and the device.
Make sure the required app is open on your device before selecting it: Ledger devices use per-coin apps (for Zcash, version 3.9.2 or later of the Zcash app), while BitBox devices, and Trezor devices for Bitcoin or Monero, need no app.
Once you see your device, select it from the menu and allow access (if applicable).

Select your desired account and name your wallet. For Zcash, there's no account to pick: name the wallet and enter its restore height or date so Cake Wallet can start scanning from there.
Then tap Next, and you will be in a view mode of your hardware wallet's account, indicated by the icon next to the wallet type.

When you connect a BitBox, Cake Wallet may show a Pairing Code screen. Check that the code matches the one shown on your BitBox, then tap Continue. If the codes don't match, close the screen to stop connecting.

A Zcash wallet added from a Ledger works a little differently from one created in Cake Wallet:
Receive: you can choose Shielded, Unified or Public addresses. The rotating Transparent and the Legacy Shielded (Sapling) address types aren't available.
 Send: sends always come from your shielded balance, and you approve each one on the Ledger.
 Shielding: ZEC received to a Public address isn't shielded automatically. Once more than 0.0003 ZEC is waiting, the home screen shows Unshielded Funds Detected. Tap it, then Shield Funds, and approve on your Ledger to move those funds into your shielded balance.
See Zcash for more about Zcash address types.

When you add a Bitcoin or Monero wallet from a Trezor, Cake Wallet shows an Almost Ready screen before it continues:
Turn on Passphrase (Optional) if this wallet has a passphrase. You can then type it in Cake Wallet under Passphrase, or turn on Enter passphrase on device to type it on the Trezor instead.
 On a Safe 7, the first time you pair you type the Pairing Code shown on the device into Cake Wallet. Cake Wallet remembers the pairing, so you aren't asked for the code again, and you may also see an Auto-connect toggle.
 Tap Skip if you don't need any of these, or Continue once you've set them.

How to restore all of your Cake Wallet wallets and settings from an encrypted backup file and its password on a fresh install with no existing wallets.
A Cake Wallet backup file restores all of your wallets and settings in one step. You'll need the backup file itself and the backup password you saved when creating the backup.
Backups can only be restored on a fresh install with no existing wallets. And ALWAYS save the mnemonic seeds for all of your wallets as well — they are your ultimate backup.
On a fresh install, tap Restore Existing Wallet on the welcome screen, then choose Backup file.

chunks.s: Enter the password and select the file
chunks.x:
Enter your backup password, tap Select backup file, and choose the backup file from your device. Then tap Import.
All of your wallets and settings will be restored.

chunks.s: I don't see the Backup file option
chunks.x: Backup file is only offered when you start from Restore Existing Wallet on the welcome screen of a fresh install. If you open the restore options from the wallet list of an app that already has wallets, it isn't shown — that's why a backup needs a fresh install.

Please select backup file and enter backup password. — You tapped Import before both choosing a file and entering the password. Do both, then tap Import again.
 This is not a valid backup file, please make sure you have selected the correct one — The file you picked isn't a Cake Wallet backup. Cake Wallet backups are .zip files whose names start with cakewalletbackup followed by the date and time they were made. Select that .zip file itself, and don't unzip or modify it.
 A Warning saying This backup was created in …, but you are restoring it in … — The backup was made in a different app (for example Monero.com) than the one you're restoring into. Double-check it's the right file: tap OK to continue anyway, or Cancel to stop.
 An Error mentioning FailedDecryption — The backup password is wrong. Use the backup password shown on the Backup page when the backup was made (or the one you set with Change password) — not your PIN. Enter it exactly, then tap Import again. Very old backups show message authentication code (MAC) instead for the same problem.
 An Error mentioning checksum mismatch, BadChecksum, BadDataLength, missing data.bin or empty file — The backup file is damaged or incomplete, for example from an interrupted download or copy. Get a fresh copy of the original file from where you stored it and try again.

Some of these errors also show technical details underneath the message. Look for the key words above to tell which problem you have.
If you can't get the backup file to restore, you can still restore each wallet from its recovery phrase — see Restore from recovery phrase or keys.

How to create a new wallet in Cake Wallet: pick a currency and seed type, write down and verify your recovery phrase, and choose where to store it safely.
Creating a wallet takes a couple of minutes. The most important part: writing down your recovery phrase — the only way to recover your funds if you lose your device.

On a fresh install, tap Create New Wallet after setting your PIN. (Adding another wallet later? Go to the Wallets tab and tap + Create New Wallet — see Wallet groups to share one recovery phrase across currencies.)
Choose the currency for this wallet. Not sure? Pick the one you plan to use first — you can add wallets for other currencies at any time.

Give the wallet a name you'll recognize (or tap the shuffle icon for a random one). This name is only visible to you.
For Monero, you can also pick the seed type — Polyseed (16 words) is the default — and the recovery phrase language. Under Advanced Settings you can add an optional BIP39 passphrase.
A passphrase is an advanced feature: it creates a completely different wallet, and a lost passphrase cannot be recovered — not even with your recovery phrase.
Want one recovery phrase to back wallets for several currencies? Choose the BIP39 seed type — only BIP39 wallets can join a wallet group. Monero's default Polyseed cannot.

chunks.s: Acknowledge the warnings, then write down your recovery phrase
chunks.x:
Before revealing anything, Cake Wallet shows a Your Secret Recovery Phrase screen with three statements you must read and tick:
that the recovery phrase is the ONLY way to recover the assets in this wallet,
 that you will write it down and store it somewhere safe outside the app,
 that you will never show or share it, because your funds can and will be stolen.
Once all three are ticked, tap Show me my Recovery Phrase, then write the words down — on paper or in a password manager — in order.
NEVER share your recovery phrase with anyone, and never type it into a website. Anyone who has it can take your funds. Cake Wallet support will never ask for it.

chunks.s: Acknowledge the warnings, then write down your recovery phrase
chunks.x: This screen also offers Skip this step. Skipping creates the wallet without ever showing you the recovery phrase, and Cake Wallet asks you to confirm before it does. If you skip, back the wallet up as soon as you can from Settings → Wallet settings → Recovery & Keys.

Tap Verify Phrase. Cake Wallet asks you to confirm two of your words (for example, "What is the 9th word of your Recovery Phrase?"). Answer from what you wrote down — that's the point of the exercise.

Tap Open Wallet and you land on your home screen, ready to receive funds. You can view your recovery phrase again any time under Settings (the gear icon at the top right) → Wallet settings → Recovery & Keys.

chunks.s: Where to keep your recovery phrase
chunks.x:
Paper in a safe place works. If you prefer a password manager, use one that is end-to-end encrypted:
| Password manager | Cost | Platforms |
| --------------------------------------- | ---- | -------------------- |
| Bitwarden | Free | Mobile, desktop, web |
| Proton Pass | Free | Mobile, desktop, web |
| KeePassXC | Free | Desktop |
| KeePassDX | Free | Android |
| 1Password | Paid | Mobile, desktop, web |
| Apple Passwords | Free | Apple devices |
Avoid storing your recovery phrase in plain notes apps, screenshots, or cloud drives without encryption.

chunks.s: Deleting and reinstalling on iPhone or iPad
chunks.x:
Cake Wallet keeps your wallets in the app's own storage on your device, so deleting the app deletes your wallets with it. Reinstalling does not bring them back: Cake Wallet starts up as a brand-new install. Any PIN, biometric unlock and Cake 2FA settings left over from the old install are cleared too, so you set the app up from scratch.
Before you delete the app, make sure you have the recovery phrase for every wallet in it. Without a recovery phrase (or a backup file and its password), a deleted wallet cannot be recovered — by you or by Cake Wallet.

Write down the recovery phrase for each wallet. See How to find my recovery phrase. For Monero and other coins that scan the blockchain, also note roughly when you created each wallet, so you can pick a restore date later.
 Optionally, export a backup file and keep it somewhere outside Cake Wallet (for example in Files or on a computer), together with its backup password. See Create a backup.

Restore your wallets in one of two ways:
From recovery phrases, one wallet at a time. See Recovery phrase or keys.
 From a backup file, all at once: on the welcome screen tap Restore Existing Wallet, then Backup file. This option is only offered on a fresh install. See Backup file.
Then let each wallet finish syncing. If a restored wallet shows 0 or is missing transactions, see Restore & backup.

If your system does not already have Flatpak installed, please do so by following the instructions on
Once Flatpak is installed (can test by running flatpak in the terminal), you will also need to install the Flathub repository by running:

flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
Now you can download the Cake Wallet Flatpak from the releases on GitHub and select the CakeWalletvX.X.X.flatpak file to download. (Example: CakeWalletv4.18.2Linux.flatpak)
Not every release includes Linux files. If the newest release doesn't list a Linux.flatpak or Linux.tar.xz file under Assets, scroll down to the most recent release that does.
Assuming the Cake Wallet flatpak is in the Downloads directory, install it with:
bash
flatpak install ~/Downloads/CakeWalletv4.18.2Linux.flatpak
(Change the version number to the one you downloaded.)
After confirming the installation, launch Cake Wallet from your shortcuts, or run it manually with:
bash
flatpak run com.cakewallet.cakewallet

Download the tar.xz release from GitHub (Example: CakeWalletv4.18.2Linux.tar.xz)
Extract the archive using your file explorer or from the terminal:
bash
tar -xf CakeWalletvX.X.X.tar.xz
Run the executable by right-clicking and selecting "Run" in your file explorer or starting it from the terminal:
bash
./cakewallet

Each GitHub release that includes Linux files lists the SHA-256 hash of every file in its release notes. After downloading, open a terminal and run:
bash
sha256sum ~/Downloads/CakeWalletvX.X.XLinux.flatpak
(Use the name of the file you downloaded, including .tar.xz for the manual install.) The output must match the hash listed for that file on the release page. If it doesn't, delete the file and download it again. The published SHA-256 hash is the way to check a Linux download; there are no separate signature files.

How to install and run Cake Wallet on Tails from Persistent Storage so your wallets and preferences survive reboots, with the exact launch command.
To use Cake Wallet on Tails, you must run Cake Wallet with extra arguments to store the wallet and preferences in your Persistent volume.
Tails is an amnesic operating system. Every time Tails is shutdown, it loses any extra programs or files you downloaded. In order to use Cake Wallet on Tails, you must set up Persistent Storage. This allows you to save the Cake Wallet installation and not need to set it up every time you restart your Tails install.
To create Persistent Storage, please see
It is recommended to put the entire Cake Wallet installation under the Persistent volume to avoid re-downloading every time Tails is started up.

Open the Tor Browser, go to https://github.com/cake-tech/cakewallet/releases/, and download the latest release. Example: CakeWalletv4.11.0Linux.tar.xz
The download will be stored at /home/amnesia/Tor Browser. Click the Download icon on the top-right, then click the Open in Folder icon to access the download folder.
Extract the Cakewallet.tar.xz into the Persistent volume at /home/amnesia/Persistent.
Example video for extracting the Cake Wallet files into a custom cakewallet Persistent directory.

Open the cakewallet folder (or whichever extracted folder has the cakewallet executable) in the Persistent volume.
Right-click on a blank area and click Open in Terminal.
Run Cake Wallet using this command:
export CAKEWALLETDIR=$HOME/Persistent/cakewallet/
XDGDATAHOME=$CAKEWALLETDIR/preferences ./cakewallet
This will place the wallets under /home/amnesia/Persistent/cakewallet/wallets and the preferences file under /home/amnesia/Persistent/cakewallet/preferences/
You can change the CAKEWALLETDIR and XDGDATAHOME to any other directory, as long as they are somewhere in your Persistent volume!
Every time you start up Tails, you can access the Persistent volume and your Cake Wallet folder by using the File Browser or the Terminal, and follow the above instructions to run Cake Wallet.

Cryptocurrencies supported in Cake Wallet: Monero, Zcash, Bitcoin, Litecoin, EVM chains, Solana, Tron, Nano and more, with how seeds, fees and tokens differ.
Cake Wallet is one non-custodial app for seventeen separate chains — privacy coins, Bitcoin and its forks, the EVM ecosystem, and several chains that don't fit any of those boxes. Every wallet you create belongs to you alone: seeds and keys are generated on your device and never leave it, so no one at Cake can see your balances, freeze your funds, or move them on your behalf.
The pages below cover what genuinely differs from one chain to the next — seed formats and derivation paths, how receive addresses behave, how fees are set, and which privacy tools apply. Pick the currency you're using and start there.

Monero — private by default. Multiple accounts and subaddresses per wallet, a choice of Polyseed, 25-word, or BIP39 seeds, and full coin control.
 Zcash — shielded transactions that hide the sender, receiver, and amount on-chain. Cake shields your funds automatically once a balance is worth shielding; very small amounts (30,000 zatoshi, or 0.0003 ZEC, or less) are left alone, since the network fee would eat most of the value.

Bitcoin — the deepest feature set in the app: Lightning, Silent Payments, Payjoin, coin control, and a fresh receive address after every use.
 Litecoin — fast, low-cost payments, with optional MWEB confidential balances on Android and iOS.
 Bitcoin Cash — larger blocks and low fees, CashAddr addresses, and coin control.
 Dogecoin — quick blocks and very low fees, which makes it popular for tips and small payments. Coin control supported.

Six EVM networks, each its own wallet type. They share the familiar 0x address format and a BIP39 seed — 12 words by default, with 24 available if you prefer — which means one seed can cover all of them in a wallet group. The same address format does not mean the same network, though — always confirm which chain a sender is using before funds are on the way.

Ethereum — the original smart contract chain. ERC-20 tokens, USDT bridging, and optional Blink MEV protection.
 Polygon — an Ethereum Layer-2 with much lower fees. Fees are paid in POL, renamed from MATIC in 2024. Supports USDT bridging.
 Arbitrum — an Ethereum Layer-2 that inherits Ethereum's security. Fees are paid in ETH. Supports USDT bridging.
 Base — an Ethereum Layer-2 built by Coinbase. Fees are paid in ETH, with optional Blink MEV protection.
 Robinhood Chain — an Ethereum Layer-2 for stablecoins and tokenized stocks. Fees are paid in ETH; USDG and USDe are shown by default.
 BNB Smart Chain — EVM-compatible with low fees and fast blocks. Uses the same ERC-20 token standard, often called BEP-20 here.

Solana — high throughput and very low fees. Holds SPL tokens, and sets the fee for you automatically.
 Tron — widely used for USDT (TRC-20). Fees work differently here: transactions consume bandwidth and energy, and the network burns a little TRX when you don't hold enough.
 Nano — feeless and near-instant, with no network fee to send at all.
 Decred — a hybrid Proof-of-Work and Proof-of-Stake chain with governance built into the protocol. Coin control supported.

Beyond native coins, you can hold tokens on all six EVM chains, on Solana (SPL), and on Tron (TRC-20). Well-known tokens are available out of the box, and anything else can be added by contract address — see Add custom tokens.
One thing worth remembering: tokens never pay their own fees. Sending USDT on Ethereum costs ETH, on Polygon it costs POL, on Tron it costs TRX, and so on. Keep a small balance of the chain's native coin so your token transfers can go through.

Some currencies we support can no longer be created. Zano is being phased out: since v6.5.0, new Zano wallets can't be created or restored, but existing ones keep working for now. Wownero wallets still open, but only to show you their seed and keys so you can recover your funds in another wallet. Haven support has also been removed. If you hold Wownero or Haven, the Wownero page walks through getting your funds out.

Which coins you can hold in Cake Wallet, which have tokens, and why swap and buy/sell availability depends on providers, your currency and region.
Holding a coin, swapping it, and buying it with fiat are three different things in Cake Wallet, and each has its own list of what's supported. In short:
Wallets are built into the app. If a wallet type is in the list below, you can create it, hold it, send and receive it.
 Swaps are done by third-party swap providers. Whether a pair works depends on what those providers support right now.
 Buying and selling with fiat is done by third-party on-ramp and off-ramp providers. Whether you can buy or sell depends on the provider, the coin, the fiat currency you pay in, and your region.

chunks.x:
Well-known tokens are available out of the box on the token-capable chains, and you can add others by contract address — see Add custom tokens. Tokens always pay their network fee in the chain's native coin, so keep a little of it in the same wallet.
Zano and Wownero are not on this list: new wallets for them can't be created. Existing Zano wallets keep working for now, and Wownero wallets open only so you can view their seed and keys. The Cake Wallet desktop builds for macOS and Linux are built without Zcash and Decred.

chunks.t: Wallets, swaps and buying by coin
chunks.x:
Cake Wallet doesn't run its own exchange. When you swap, it asks its swap providers for quotes and shows you the best one. In v6.5.0 those providers are ChangeNOW, Chainflip, SwapTrade, XOSwap, Swaps.XYZ, Jupiter, Near Intents and Trocador (an aggregator that routes to other exchanges).
That means:
The swap lists are broader than the wallet list. The Send and Receive pickers on the Swap screen include many assets Cake Wallet can't hold, plus tokens from your EVM, Solana and Tron wallets. To receive an asset you don't have a Cake wallet for, use Select Receiver to enter an address from another wallet.
 Being in the list doesn't guarantee a pair works. Support is checked live, for the exact pair and amount you enter. A provider is used only if it supports that pair, the amount is within its minimum and maximum, and — with Fixed rate on — it offers fixed-rate swaps.

chunks.t: Wallets, swaps and buying by coin
chunks.x:
To check a pair, pick the two assets on the Swap screen and enter an amount. When a provider can do it, the bar below shows the provider's name and the rate. If it stays on Finding provider..., none of the providers is quoting that pair at that amount right now. Try a different amount, turn off Fixed rate, or try again later.
If you set Swap to Tor only under Settings → Connections, only Trocador is used, so fewer pairs are available. See Privacy settings.
For a full walkthrough, see Swap.

chunks.t: Wallets, swaps and buying by coin
chunks.s: Buying and selling depends on the provider and where you are
chunks.x:
Buying and selling with fiat is handled by third-party providers. In v6.5.0, Cake Wallet offers Robinhood Connect, DFX.swiss, Onramper, MoonPay and Kriptonim for buying, and DFX.swiss, Onramper, MoonPay and Kriptonim for selling. Each provider supports its own set of coins, fiat currencies, payment methods and countries, and Cake Wallet has no control over that.
To check what's available to you:
1. Open the wallet you want to buy into (or sell from), tap Buy on its balance card, then choose Buy Crypto or Sell Crypto.
2. Pick the asset and the fiat currency. The asset picker offers the open wallet's coin and the tokens in that wallet, so to buy a different coin, switch to that wallet first.
3. Continue to see the providers. Cake Wallet only asks providers that support that coin and fiat currency, and lists the quotes under Available Providers.

chunks.s: Buying or swapping never creates a wallet
chunks.x:
Cake Wallet doesn't create a wallet for you when you buy, swap or pay. New wallets only appear in the Wallets tab when you create or restore one yourself.
Buy sends the coins to the wallet you have open, using an address from that wallet.
 Swap asks where to send the coins under Select Receiver. The list shows only wallets you already have for that coin — or You have no wallets for that coin — and you can enter an address from another wallet instead.
 Payment links that need a different network can switch you to a compatible wallet you already have (Switch to … Wallet) or offer a swap. If you have neither, Cake Wallet tells you that you need a wallet for that network.

To buy or receive a coin you don't have a wallet for yet, create the wallet first from the Wallets tab with + Create New Wallet. A new wallet comes with its own recovery phrase to back up — unless you add it to an existing wallet group with Choose Wallet Group, so it shares a recovery phrase you've already backed up.
