Send and receive Bitcoin over Lightning in Cake Wallet via Spark: get a cake.cash address, move funds to and from on-chain, and understand the privacy limits.
Lightning lets you send and receive Bitcoin instantly, with fees measured in fractions of a cent — perfect for everyday payments where waiting for on-chain confirmations doesn't make sense.
Cake Wallet's Lightning support is powered by Spark, a new Bitcoin scaling network, through the Breez SDK. What that means for you: it's self-custodial and there are no channels to open, manage, or rebalance — it just works. The honest tradeoff: your Lightning balance lives on the Spark network rather than on the Bitcoin chain itself, so treat it like a spending balance and keep larger amounts on-chain.
Lightning is available on Bitcoin wallets on mobile and macOS (not Windows/Linux), and is enabled by default. You can turn it off under Settings → Privacy → Enable Lightning.

Your Bitcoin wallet's home screen has two chips at the top left: the Bitcoin chip for your on-chain balance, and the ⚡ chip for Lightning. Tap ⚡ to see your Lightning balance (shown in sats) with Deposit and Withdraw buttons.
Tap Receive, tap the address type under the QR code, and choose Lightning.

Your wallet gets a Lightning address — like carrotcake@cake.cash — that anyone can pay from any Lightning wallet, any amount, any time. Share it as text or let them scan the QR. Use Set amount to request a specific amount instead.

You can receive Lightning payments with a zero balance, on a wallet you created a minute ago. Nothing to set up, no minimum, no waiting on an on-chain transaction first. Tap Receive, share your Lightning address, and the sats arrive.
This is the part of classic Lightning that Spark fixes completely. On an ordinary Lightning wallet you can only receive what your channels have room for, so your first payment usually means opening a channel and paying an on-chain fee for the privilege. Spark has no channels, so there's no inbound liquidity to run out of — the incoming Lightning payment is atomically swapped into Spark sats you own, and you never have to borrow capacity from anyone.
Payments land while you're offline. Spark can complete an incoming Lightning payment without your wallet being online — one of the reasons it works well on a phone. Close the app, get paid, and the payment is waiting for you when you next open the wallet.

Every Bitcoin wallet with Lightning turned on gets a username straight away. Each time the wallet opens, Cake Wallet asks for the Lightning address already registered to it, and only if there isn't one does it register a random name (a generated name followed by a number). Right after you create a new Bitcoin wallet and back up its seed, Cake Wallet shows the Lightning Username screen so you can pick your own name, or tap Skip to keep the random one.
You can change it any time under Settings → Bitcoin Settings → Lightning Username → Change Username. Type a custom name or tap the shuffle icon for a random one, then tap Confirm. Usernames can use lowercase letters a-z, numbers 0-9, -, and ., and must be 1 to 64 characters long. The screen shows Username Available when the name is free and This username is not available. when someone else has it. Your username becomes your yourname@cake.cash address.

One address at a time. After you change your username, your Receive screen and QR code show only the new address, and Cake Wallet has no option to keep the old name alongside it. Update the address anywhere you've shared or published the old one.
 No expiry, release or transfer in the app. Cake Wallet has no renewal step for usernames, and no option to delete one, release it, or move it to a different wallet. The only change you can make is picking a new name for the same wallet.
 Turning Lightning off doesn't unregister it. Switching off Enable Lightning stops Lightning in the app but leaves your username registered. When you turn Lightning back on, Cake Wallet looks up the address registered to your wallet again.
 It comes back when you restore. Your username is tied to your seed, not your phone. Restore the same seed and the restored wallet finds the address already registered to it and keeps it, instead of generating a new random name. The username screen isn't shown after a restore, so check Settings → Bitcoin Settings → Lightning Username to see it.
 Use the same passphrase. If your seed has a passphrase, your Lightning wallet comes from the seed and passphrase together. Restoring with a different passphrase, or none, gives a different Lightning wallet with a different username.
 Same seed, same address. The same seed on two devices shares one Lightning address. If you change the username on one, the other shows the new name the next time it opens the wallet. A different seed always gets its own, separate address.

Sending works from the same Send screen as on-chain Bitcoin: paste or scan a Lightning invoice or a Lightning address, and Cake Wallet routes the payment over Lightning automatically. Payments settle in seconds — ordinary Lightning sends and receives never wait for on-chain confirmations.

Short answer: you need sats in your Lightning balance to send over Lightning. A Lightning send spends from that balance — if it's empty there's nothing to spend, and Cake Wallet won't quietly reach into your on-chain coins to cover it.
There is a way around it. Swap treats Lightning as its own asset, so you can set Send to on-chain Bitcoin (or any other coin you hold), set Receive to Lightning, and use Select Receiver to point at the recipient's Lightning address. The swap provider delivers the Lightning payment on your behalf.

It works, but it's the wrong tool for a payment. A swap routes your money through a third-party provider that sees both sides of the trade, charges a fee and a spread on top of normal network fees, and enforces a minimum trade size that most everyday Lightning payments fall below. It isn't fast either: the on-chain leg has to confirm first, which gives up the one thing you came to Lightning for. And on a floating rate the amount that lands may not match the amount that was requested — enough to fail an invoice, which can expire while the swap is still in flight.
Do this instead: deposit once, in an amount that covers what you expect to spend, and send normally from then on. Deposits wait for six confirmations, so fund your balance before you need it. If you want sats in your Lightning balance right now, the fastest route is to have someone pay you over Lightning — that lands in seconds.

Use the Deposit and Withdraw buttons on the Lightning balance view:
Deposit to Lightning — moves on-chain BTC into your Lightning balance. The sheet shows the network fee estimate up front, and Advanced Settings includes Coin Control for choosing which outputs to use.
 Withdraw to on-chain — moves sats from Lightning back to your on-chain Bitcoin balance, as an on-chain transaction.
Six confirmations applies only to moving funds in and out of Lightning. Deposits and withdrawals bridge between the Bitcoin chain and Spark, so both wait for six on-chain confirmations before the funds land on the other side — and deposits pay a normal on-chain fee. Sending and receiving on Lightning is unaffected: Lightning-to-Lightning payments are instant and never wait for confirmations. Small, frequent moves add up in fees — deposit what you plan to spend.

Moving payments off-chain is not the same as making them private. The model is closer to a VPN than to a public ledger: your activity leaves Bitcoin's permanent, world-readable history, but the network's operators can still see it. What matters is what happens to that data next — and that's where Cake Wallet's defaults do the work.

Every Spark transfer is co-signed by the Spark Operators — a small, permissioned set of companies that run the network, a threshold of which must sign for any transfer to go through. Co-signing means they see the transfer: the amount, and the Spark addresses on either end. That's inherent to how Spark works, and no wallet can opt out of it.
What a wallet can control is whether that data travels any further. Cake Wallet makes two choices on your behalf, both on by default with nothing for you to configure:

Your Spark transactions are never published to public Spark explorers. Other Spark wallets publish by default, which makes balances and history searchable by anyone who has your address. Yours aren't — the barista you paid this morning can't look up what else is in your wallet.
 Your Spark address is never embedded in your Lightning invoices. The default Spark SDKs include it, so anyone holding a single invoice of yours could decode it and pull up your entire Spark history. Cake Wallet leaves it out.

Better than on-chain Bitcoin. There's no permanent public record of your Lightning payments for anyone to scrape, cluster, and re-examine years from now.
 Not cryptographic privacy. This is a small set of operators choosing not to publish what they can see, not math that stops them seeing it. When you need privacy that doesn't rest on anyone's promise, use Monero, or Silent Payments on-chain.

Your Lightning address is a permanent identifier. yourname@cake.cash is reusable by design, exactly like an email address — everyone you hand it to can link every payment they send you, and the server answering for it sees those requests. For a payment you'd rather not tie to a name you use publicly, generate a one-off invoice with Set amount instead.
 Deposits and withdrawals are ordinary Bitcoin transactions. They're permanently public, and they link specific on-chain coins to the act of funding a Lightning balance. Coin control lets you choose which coins do that.
 Spark addresses are static today. There's no address rotation yet, so whatever is tied to one address stays tied to it.
Confidential amounts for Spark transfers are in development. Until they land, the honest summary is the same as everywhere else on this page: Lightning here is spending money, savings belong on-chain, and a payment isn't invisible just because it never touched a block explorer.

AnyPay in Cake Wallet lets you pay any supported address with the coin you already hold, swapping it into the coin the recipient wants in one send flow.
You have Monero. The person you owe wants Bitcoin. Normally you would switch wallets, or ask them for a different address. AnyPay removes that friction: pay any supported address using whatever coin you already hold. The conversion happens under the hood.

When you paste or scan a payment address, Cake Wallet detects which coin it belongs to. If it doesn't match your current wallet, AnyPay offers to swap your holdings into the coin the recipient wants and complete the payment in one flow — or, if you already have a wallet in that coin, to switch to it instead.
You approve the conversion and the send together. No manual wallet juggling.
On any wallet, tap Send and paste (or scan) the recipient's address.

Cake Wallet detects the address is for a different coin and asks what to do. Here, a Monero address pasted into a Bitcoin wallet shows "Monero Address Detected" with two choices: Switch to Monero Wallet (use a Monero wallet you already have) or Swap from Bitcoin (convert your BTC to XMR for this payment).
If you have more than one Monero wallet, switching first asks which one to use. If you have no Monero wallet at all, swapping is the only option offered.

If you swap, the Swap screen opens with the recipient already set as the destination and the amount they need locked in. Change the coin you fund the payment with under From, or tap the provider in the footer to pick a different one. Review the amount and rate, then continue to complete the swap and the payment together.

An address that starts with 0x is valid on Ethereum, Polygon, Base, Arbitrum, BNB Smart Chain and every other EVM chain, so the address alone doesn't say which network the recipient wants.
Paste one into a non-EVM wallet and Cake Wallet asks first: EVM Address Detected — pick the recipient's network, then switch or swap as above.
 In an EVM wallet, the Send screen shows the recipient's network under the address as on Ethereum. Tap it to change networks: your current network is listed first, with the other compatible networks below.
Payment links carry the network and token with them, so those are filled in for you. If a link asks for a chain or token Cake Wallet doesn't support, it tells you instead of sending to the wrong place.
Always confirm the network with the recipient. Funds sent on a chain the recipient isn't watching can be lost.

chunks.s: What to expect on rates and fees
chunks.x:
The conversion runs through Cake Wallet's swap providers — the same ones behind the Swap feature. That means:
Fixed-amount swaps are always used to ensure that the recipient gets exactly the amount of crypto they need.
 A swap fee applies on top of the network fee for the send.
 Coverage depends on which swap pairs the providers support, and swaps have minimum amounts.
We recommend reviewing the quoted rate and fee before you approve.
Both coins — the one you hold and the one the recipient wants — must be supported in Cake Wallet for AnyPay to work right now, but we'll be expanding sending support to all cryptocurrencies our swap partners support very soon.

chunks.s: Which coins can fund a payment
chunks.x: Any coin you can swap in Cake Wallet can fund an AnyPay payment. In practice the address detector recognizes Bitcoin, Litecoin, Monero, Ethereum and other EVM chains, Solana, and Tron. For an 0x recipient you also choose the network, since the same address exists on every EVM chain.

Bridge USDT between Ethereum, Polygon and Arbitrum in Cake Wallet with USDT0, paying fees in the source chain's native coin. Transfers take 2 to 30 minutes.
USDT lives on many networks, and the one you hold it on isn't always the one you need it on — maybe your funds sit on Ethereum, but the person or service you're paying only takes USDT on Arbitrum. Bridging moves USDT between supported chains directly inside Cake Wallet: no exchange account, no separate bridge website, no juggling wrapped tokens.
Bridging supports USDT only, powered by USDT0 — Tether's own system for moving USDT across chains — and only between Ethereum, Polygon and Arbitrum.
There is no Bridge action on Base, BNB Smart Chain, Tron or Solana wallets, and no other token can be bridged. To move value across any other pair of chains or assets, use a regular swap.

chunks.s: Tap USDT in your asset list
chunks.x: On an Ethereum, Polygon or Arbitrum wallet, open the Assets tab on the home screen and tap USDT.
The token sheet shows Send, Swap, Bridge, and Receive — tap Bridge.
Type how much USDT to move, or tap Max, then continue.

chunks.s: Pick the destination and receiving address
chunks.x: Choose the network to bridge to — one of the other two supported chains — then where the USDT should arrive. Tap Input an Address to paste or type the destination address; if you have a wallet on that network, it appears here too so you can pick it directly.

Check the amount, the source and destination networks, the receiving address, and the fee — then Swipe to bridge. The USDT arrives on the destination chain as native USDT.
A bridge takes between 2 and 30 minutes, depending on how congested the networks are. Track past transfers under Bridge history (the history icon on the amount screen).
You pay the bridge fee in the source chain's native coin — for example, you need a little ETH in the wallet to bridge USDT away from Ethereum. Without it, the bridge can't be signed. Fees and timing vary with network congestion.

Supported chains: Ethereum, Polygon and Arbitrum. Those are the only three networks USDT0 bridging covers in Cake Wallet, in either direction.
 Expect 2 to 30 minutes. Bridges are not instant — where a given transfer lands in that range depends on network congestion.
 Bridging works for payments, not just yourself. The receiving address can be anyone's — pay a person on Polygon straight from your Ethereum USDT. Just double-check the address and network: the recipient must actually use USDT on the chain you pick.
 USDT only. Other tokens don't offer the Bridge action; converting between different assets across chains is a regular swap.
 Check the receiving network before confirming — the whole point is choosing where the USDT ends up.

Use the Cake Wallet Charts tab to follow live and historical crypto prices, set a favorite asset, sort your followed list, and control fetching with Fiat API.
The Charts tab, the last tab in the bar at the bottom of the home screen, shows live and historical prices for the assets you choose to follow.

The large chart at the top shows your favorite asset — Bitcoin unless you pick another — with its current price and how much it has moved over the selected range. Choose a range with 1H, 1D, 7D, 30D, 1Y or ALL; the chart opens on 30D each time you visit the tab. Prices are shown in your selected fiat currency.

Below the chart, Followed assets lists every asset you follow. Bitcoin, Monero and Ethereum are followed to start with.
Tap + to follow another asset.
 Tap the sort button to order the list by Marketcap, Gains, Losses or Alphabetical.
 Long-press an asset to make it your Favorite (shown in the top chart) or to Remove it. You always keep at least one followed asset.
 Tap an asset to open its own chart, with shortcuts to Swap it, set it as your Favorite, and — if your open wallet holds it — Buy or Sell it.
Pull down on the page to refresh prices.

Price data comes from Cake Wallet's price server, the same one that provides the fiat value of your balances. The server sees which assets you follow, not your wallets or balances. Price history is stored on your device, so only missing data is requested.
Charts follow your Fiat API setting under Settings → Connections:
Enabled — prices are fetched normally (through Tor if built-in Tor is on).
 Tor only — prices are fetched from Cake's onion service.
 Disabled — Charts is turned off and the tab shows Charts unavailable.

Connect Cake Wallet to dApps with WalletConnect on Ethereum, Polygon, Base, Arbitrum, BNB Smart Chain, Robinhood Chain and Solana, and sign safely.
WalletConnect links Cake Wallet to decentralized apps (dApps) — exchanges, NFT marketplaces, lending apps and more — running in a browser or on another device. The dApp asks for permission to see your address and sends you requests to sign; nothing is signed or sent until you approve it in Cake Wallet. Your keys never leave the app.

WalletConnect works with these wallet types:
| Wallet | Network ID WalletConnect uses |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Ethereum | eip155:1 |
| Polygon | eip155:137 |
| Base | eip155:8453 |
| Arbitrum | eip155:42161 |
| BNB Smart Chain | eip155:56 |
| Robinhood Chain | eip155:4663 |
| Solana | Solana mainnet |
WalletConnect is not available for hardware wallets. If you open a WalletConnect link while a wallet of another type (for example Bitcoin or Monero) is open, Cake Wallet asks you to switch to one of the wallets above and try again.

Open the wallet you want to connect, then go to Settings → Settings → WalletConnect — for example Settings → Ethereum Settings → WalletConnect, or Settings → Solana Settings → WalletConnect.
The WalletConnect screen lists the dApps already connected to this wallet. If none are connected yet, it reads Active connections will appear here.
On the dApp's website, choose Connect wallet (the wording varies by dApp) and pick WalletConnect. The dApp shows a QR code and usually a button to copy the link.

chunks.s: Scan it or paste it into Cake Wallet
chunks.x:
On the WalletConnect screen, choose one:
Scan QR — point your camera at the dApp's QR code. This button appears on iOS and Android only.
 Paste WalletConnect link — opens Enter WalletConnect URI. Paste the link you copied from the dApp (the paste icon fills it from your clipboard), then tap Confirm.
You can also tap Scan on your wallet's home screen and scan the dApp's WalletConnect QR code directly — Cake Wallet recognizes it and opens WalletConnect for you.

A Connect request sheet shows:
the dApp's name, icon and web address, with would like to connect
 a Verified or Not Verified badge, based on WalletConnect's domain check
 the wallet and address you are about to share
 what the dApp is asking to do — always View your wallet balance and activity, plus Request approval for transactions, Sign messages and typed data and Switch and add EVM chains when the dApp asks for them
If WalletConnect flags the dApp as a known scam, a red WARNING! banner appears: This request appears to be from a known scam. Please proceed with caution.

Swipe to approve to connect. To refuse, tap the X in the top-left corner of the sheet — the dApp is told you rejected the request.
Once connected, the dApp appears in your WalletConnect list. You can go back to the dApp in your browser.

Every time a connected dApp wants something signed, Cake Wallet shows a sheet for you to review. You can approve it or tap the X to reject it.
Transactions open as Approve request. On EVM networks the message lists the Value being sent and the From and To addresses, along with the Network fee or Max network fee (with a fiat estimate when a price is available). On Solana the sheet shows the transaction data the dApp sent. Swipe to approve to sign it.
 Messages and typed data (for example a "Sign in with Ethereum" message or a token permit) open as Signing request, showing the Message to sign. Swipe Swipe to sign to sign it. When a dApp sends several sign-in messages at once, a Sign all messages button also appears.

Each request also shows the Method, Chain ID and Transport Type the dApp used, plus the wallet name and address that will sign. After you approve or reject, Cake Wallet returns you to the dApp where it can, or shows a confirmation such as You can go back to your dApp now.
With VoiceOver or TalkBack turned on, the swipe control appears as a regular labeled button (Approve or Confirm), so connection and signing requests can be approved with a screen reader.

chunks.s: Connections stay with the wallet that approved them
chunks.x:
A WalletConnect connection belongs to the wallet (address) you approved it from. The WalletConnect list only shows the dApps connected to the wallet that is currently open, and switching to another wallet in Cake Wallet does not hand an existing dApp connection over to it.
If a dApp sends a request for a different wallet than the one you have open, Cake Wallet rejects it and shows: This request was made for a different wallet. Open the wallet connected to this app and try again. Switch back to the wallet you connected with and repeat the action on the dApp.

1. Open the WalletConnect screen (Settings → Settings → WalletConnect).
2. Tap a dApp in the list. Its details page shows Connected to , when the connection Expires on, the wallet and address it can see, and the permissions you granted.
3. To disconnect, tap Delete, then confirm Delete in the prompt.
The dApp loses access immediately. To use it again, connect from scratch.

Check the web address. On every connection and signing request, compare the dApp's address shown under its name with the site you meant to visit. Treat Not Verified with caution and never continue past a WARNING! scam banner unless you are certain.
 Read before you swipe. Check the amount, destination address and network fee on every transaction. If you don't understand what a message or transaction does, reject it — a single signature can be enough to approve someone to move your tokens.
 Connect only what you need. Disconnect dApps you no longer use from the WalletConnect list.
 Never paste your recovery phrase into a dApp. WalletConnect never needs it. Anyone asking for it is trying to steal your funds — see What to do if scammed.
 Consider a separate wallet with only the funds you need for dApps, and keep your savings in another wallet.

How to view, switch, rename and delete wallets on the Cake Wallet Wallets screen, including shared and single seed wallets and backing up before you delete.
Cake Wallet lets you keep as many wallets as you like on a single device and switch between them at any time. This page covers the Wallets screen: viewing your wallets, switching between them, renaming a wallet, and deleting one.

Tap the Wallets tab in the bottom navigation bar to see all of your wallets. They are organized into two sections:
Shared Seed Wallets — wallets that were created together from a single seed as part of a wallet group.
 Single Seed Wallets — wallets that each have their own separate seed.
From this screen you can also tap Create New Wallet to add a new wallet, or Restore Wallet to bring in an existing one.
Tap any wallet in the list to make it your active wallet. Cake switches to that wallet and returns you to the home screen, where its balance and transaction history are shown.
Tap the pencil icon next to a wallet to open the Edit wallet screen. Enter a new name, then tap Save.

To delete a wallet, open the Edit wallet screen (tap the pencil next to the wallet), tap the red Delete button, and confirm on the prompt.
Deleting a wallet removes it and its transaction history from this device. If you have not backed up that wallet's seed (or private keys), any funds it holds will be lost permanently — neither Cake nor anyone else can recover them. Always make sure you have a working backup before deleting a wallet you might need again.
Once you confirm, the wallet is removed from your list. Your other wallets are unaffected.

Wallet groups in Cake Wallet let one BIP39 recovery phrase back a wallet for each currency, like Bitcoin and Ethereum. How to add, manage and restore a group.
A wallet group lets one recovery phrase back a wallet for each currency you use — write down one set of words, and you've backed up your Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, and more. Each group can hold a single wallet of each currency type.
Only BIP39 wallets can share a recovery phrase. Monero wallets created with the default Polyseed (16 words) or legacy (25 words) seed can't join a group — if you want your Monero wallet in a group, create it with the BIP39 seed type instead. To see how Cake Wallet derives Monero keys from a BIP39 phrase and how to restore that wallet elsewhere, see How BIP39 Monero wallets work.
Open the Wallets tab from the bottom bar and tap + Create New Wallet, then pick the currency you want to add.
Cake Wallet asks whether this wallet should share a recovery phrase with an existing wallet (Choose Wallet Group) or get a brand-new one (Create New Recovery Phrase).

Select the group (or wallet) you want to share a recovery phrase with and tap Next.
If Cake Wallet says you don't have any compatible wallet groups, your existing wallets use seed types that can't be shared (for example, a Polyseed Monero wallet) — tap Create New Recovery Phrase to start a BIP39 group instead.

Name the new wallet and tap Next. Because it shares an existing recovery phrase, there's nothing new to write down — Cake Wallet confirms you're reusing a recovery phrase you've already backed up, with the option to verify it again.
The Wallets tab lists your wallets under Shared Seed Wallets (grouped, e.g. "Wallet Group 1") and Single Seed Wallets. Tap the pencil icon to rename a group or a wallet.

chunks.s: Merging groups or moving a wallet
chunks.x:
Groups can't be merged, and a wallet can't be moved from one group to another. Cake Wallet groups wallets by their recovery phrase, so a wallet with a different phrase can't join a group. The pencil icon only lets you rename a group or a wallet, or delete a wallet.
To bring your funds together in one group:
1. Pick the group you want to keep, and make sure its recovery phrase is backed up.
2. For each currency that group is missing, tap + Create New Wallet, pick the currency, then Choose Wallet Group and select that group (see Add a wallet to a group). A group holds only one wallet of each currency, so if it already has one, use that wallet.
3. Send the funds from each old wallet to the matching wallet in the group you're keeping. These are normal transactions, so network fees apply.

chunks.s: Merging groups or moving a wallet
chunks.x: Keep the old recovery phrase until every old wallet is empty and the transfers have confirmed. Only then delete the old wallets if you no longer want them.

One recovery phrase restores every wallet in the group: restore it once for any currency, then add the other currencies to the same group with Create New Wallet → Choose Wallet Group — no extra words to keep track of.
Back up the group's recovery phrase once and keep it safe — it controls every wallet in the group. See Create backup for full-app backups.

How to create an encrypted Cake Wallet backup file of all wallets and settings, save the backup password, and store the file on a flash drive or Proton Drive.
A Cake Wallet backup copies all of your wallets and settings so they can be restored into a fresh Cake Wallet installation. Backups can only be restored on a new install with no existing wallets. To restore from a backup, see Restore from a backup file.
ALWAYS save the mnemonic seeds for all of your wallets as well — a backup file complements your seeds, it doesn't replace them.

Open Settings from the top right of the home screen, then under App settings tap Backup. You will be prompted for your PIN, biometric authentication, or password (plus TOTP if you require 2FA for backup settings).

The Backup page shows a securely-generated backup password. Tap it to copy it.
SAVE THIS PASSWORD. Store it with the same care as a seed phrase — the backup is useless without it.
Once you have saved it, tap Export backup and confirm with Yes, I have. It can take a few moments to create the backup file, so don't panic if the screen freezes for up to a minute.
Alternatively, you can set your own encryption password with Change password. This is NOT recommended.

What happens next depends on your platform:
Android — you are asked to pick a destination: Share hands the file to the OS share sheet, Save to Downloads writes it to your Downloads folder.
 iOS — the share sheet opens directly; there is no Save to Downloads choice.
 Desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux) — a file-save dialog opens so you can choose where to write the file.
You now have a backup file!

It's easy to keep an encrypted backup on flash storage!
You will need a flash drive with a USB-C, micro-USB, or Lightning connector, depending on your device. Modern Android phones and recent iPhones use USB-C; older iPhones use a Lightning connector.
We recommend buying a flash drive from a reputable merchant, such as a large brick-and-mortar retail store or online directly from the manufacturer. 1 GB or more of storage is plenty. This should cost you about $5–20.
After you have the flash drive, plug it into your device.
Follow steps 1 to 3 above. On Android, for step 4 tap Save to Downloads, then copy the file to your flash drive using your device's file manager. On iOS, pick your file manager or the drive itself from the share sheet; on desktop, save straight to the drive in the file-save dialog.
That's it! Make sure you have the password!

Proton Drive allows you to save end-to-end encrypted backups to the cloud. Proton doesn't know the contents of your uploaded files.
First create a Proton account. A free plan includes 1 GB of storage, which is enough for at least 1 backup.
Follow steps 1 to 3 above. On Android, for step 4 tap Share and then Proton Drive (it may be hidden under More); on iOS the share sheet opens on its own, so just pick Proton Drive there.
After you tap Proton Drive, optionally go to the location in your encrypted cloud drive where you would like to upload the backup file. Tap Upload.
Share, More and Upload are labels from your operating system's share sheet and the Proton Drive app, not from Cake Wallet, so they may differ on your device.
That's it! Make sure you have the password!

How to rescan your wallet in Cake Wallet when transactions are missing: open Settings, Connections, pick a restore date or block height, and let history reload.
Rescanning will remove any saved transaction keys and destination addresses, which may be useful for proving payments.
If your XMR transaction is still not appearing and the wallet has already finished syncing, then you can rescan by opening Settings in the top-right, tapping Connections, then tapping Rescan.

Open Settings from the top-right, tap Connections, then tap the Rescan button.
The Rescan button under Connections is shown for Monero, Zcash and Decred wallets.

chunks.s: Choose a restore date or block height
chunks.x: For Monero and Zcash wallets, Cake Wallet fills in the block height with the restore height saved for this wallet, which is usually the right starting point — only change it if you know your first transaction is older. Otherwise, enter a date or a block height from about a week before you created this wallet. For example, if the wallet was created in February 2020 you could use January 31st, 2020 as the "restore from date." Alternatively, use the "Height" shown for your wallet's very first transaction and enter that number as the "Block height."

chunks.s: Choose a restore date or block height
chunks.x: After entering the date and tapping Rescan, leave the Cake Wallet app open with your phone awake while the wallet rescans the blocks for transactions involving your wallet. When the rescan starts, your transaction history will disappear and your balance will read as 0.0 XMR. As the wallet continues scanning blocks, your transaction history will reappear one transaction at a time. When the rescan is completed, the sync progress status and indicator at the top of the balance screen will disappear and your entire transaction history and proper balance will be restored.

How to switch nodes or add a custom node in Cake Wallet, with SSL, Trusted and SOCKS proxy options, and why your own Monero or Bitcoin node maximizes privacy.
Your wallet doesn't hold the blockchain — it connects to a node that does. The node you use decides who sees your wallet's network activity, which makes this setting worth two minutes of your time: Cake Wallet's defaults work out of the box, and pointing the app at your own node gives you the strongest privacy available.

Each currency has its own node list. Open Settings from the top right, tap your wallet's coin settings (for example Bitcoin Settings), then tap Nodes.
The current node is marked, and Cake Wallet ships several presets per currency. Tap another node to switch to it; use the refresh icon to re-test the list.
If your wallet won't connect or sync, switching nodes is the first fix to try — see Resolving connection issues.

These are the Monero nodes Cake Wallet v6.5.0 ships with. Cake Wallet is the default.
| Node label | Address | Notes |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Cake Wallet | xmr-node.cakewallet.com:18081 | Default. Cake Wallet's own node, SSL. |
| Cake Wallet (Tor) | cakexmrkbd7ptshw7vfzhzqgg77xgeavdrxm6zbu57lppfkj3fczbrqd.onion:18081 | Cake Wallet's onion node. Only connects while Tor is on — see Built-in Tor. |
| Seth For Privacy | node.sethforprivacy.com:443 | SSL |
| MoneroDevs | node.monerodevs.org:18089 | SSL |
| MoneroDevs #2 | node2.monerodevs.org:18089 | SSL |
| MoneroDevs #3 | node3.monerodevs.org:18089 | SSL |
| Feather Wallet | selsta1.featherwallet.net:18081 | SSL |
| StormyCloud | xmr.stormycloud.org:18089 | SSL |
This list can change between releases, so the Nodes screen in your app is always the up-to-date version. None of these is required: you can add any Monero node you like, including your own, as described below.

Node label — any name you'll recognize.
 Node Address and Node port — e.g. node.example.com and 18081 (Monero clearnet) or 50002 (Electrum-style over SSL). Add login and password only if your node requires them.
 Use SSL — on if your node serves TLS (most public nodes on ports like 18089/50002 do).
 Trusted — turn on ONLY for a node you control. It tells the wallet to skip some defensive checks for faster syncing.
 Use SOCKS Proxy — route this node's connection through a proxy (for example Orbot's 127.0.0.1:9050 for Tor; see Tor with Orbot).
Save, then tap your node in the list to switch to it. If it shows as unreachable, double-check the port and SSL setting — the most common mismatch is SSL enabled on a non-SSL port or vice versa.

Using someone else's node means that operator can see your wallet's queries. Running your own removes that trust entirely — it's the single biggest privacy upgrade available:
Monero: guides.monero.com and sethforprivacy.com/guides/run-a-monero-node
 Bitcoin/Litecoin: any Electrum-compatible server (Fulcrum, electrs)

Nano/Banano wallets have a separate Manage PoW nodes list under Settings → Connections (proof-of-work generation).
 Litecoin MWEB uses its own node, set under Settings → Litecoin Settings → MWEB → MWEB Node.
 During wallet creation, the Privacy settings screen lets you set a custom node before the wallet ever connects anywhere.
What your wallet recovery phrase and private keys are, and how to view them in Cake Wallet under Settings, Recovery & Keys so you can write them down safely.

Your keys encode the private information in your wallet and are what allow you to spend coins and see incoming transactions. You may also use a wallet's keys to restore the wallet.
General terms specific to public-key cryptography where a private key and a public key make up a keypair. A public key is derived from the private key.
The public key is safe to share, and gives the recipient the ability to encrypt something or verify a signature.
 The private key gives the owner the ability to sign or decrypt something, and as such, should be kept private.

Your recovery phrase (also called a seed phrase) is just a version of your private key written in a way that’s easier for you to write down. Your recovery phrase and keys are actually the same things, just in different forms! You can use a wallet's recovery phrase to restore your wallet too.

chunks.s: Viewing your wallet's recovery phrase and keys
chunks.x:
Tap the gear icon at the top right of the home screen to open Settings. Then, in the section named after your wallet, tap Recovery & Keys.
Cake Wallet warns you that secret information is about to be shown. Tap Show my Recovery Phrase & Keys, then authenticate with your PIN, biometrics, or password.
On the next screen you will see your wallet's recovery phrase and keys, split across tabs — Recovery Phrase, Keys, and a per-currency third tab such as Silent Payments (Bitcoin) or Legacy (Monero). Cake Wallet has 1 set of these per wallet, so you must save them all individually.
DO NOT show your recovery phrase or keys to anyone. Your funds will likely be stolen if you give out either.
Please write down your recovery phrase and keys and store them in a safe place. This will allow you to restore your wallet if you lose your device, or otherwise cannot access the wallet.

chunks.s: Bitcoin and Litecoin extended public key (xPub)
chunks.x:
Bitcoin and Litecoin wallets show an extended public key, labelled xPub, on the Keys tab. To find it, open Recovery & Keys as described above, switch to the Keys tab, and tap the copy icon next to xPub.
The same tab can also list Master fingerprint, WIF, Private key and Public key. Hardware wallets and watch-only wallets have no private keys in Cake Wallet, so they show only Public key and xPub. Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin wallets show an xPub too.
Only copy the xPub entry. WIF and Private key on the same tab can spend your funds, so never share them. The Show QR button on the Recovery Phrase tab encodes your recovery phrase, not your xPub, so don't use it to share your xPub.
You can import your xPub into another wallet app as a watch-only wallet. The app can then show your balance and incoming transactions, but it can't spend anything.

Cake Wallet always shows the key with the standard xpub prefix. It never uses zpub, even though Bitcoin and Litecoin wallets use native SegWit addresses by default. If the other app asks for an address or script type, choose native SegWit (P2WPKH). Litecoin wallets on a Ledger or Trezor are the exception: their key is shown in Ltub format.

The xPub belongs to your wallet's derivation path. That's m/84'/0'/0' for a BIP39 Bitcoin wallet and m/84'/2'/0' for a BIP39 Litecoin wallet. It covers the standard addresses of your first account only. It does not include:
additional Bitcoin accounts
 on BIP39 wallets, address types you pick under More Options, such as Taproot or Legacy, because each one uses its own derivation path
 Silent Payments, Lightning, or Litecoin MWEB
An xPub can't spend your coins, but it's a privacy risk. Anyone who has it can see every address it covers, along with your balance and full transaction history for those addresses. Share it only with apps and services you trust.

How to use the Cake Wallet address book to save contacts with addresses for multiple currencies, pick them when sending, and transfer between your own wallets.
Cake Wallet includes an address book that lets you save the people and addresses you send to most, so you never have to copy-paste an address twice. Tap the Contacts tab in the bottom navigation bar to open it — the screen itself is titled Address Book.
Contacts can hold addresses for multiple currencies, and the Wallets tab lists the addresses of your own wallets for quick transfers between them.
When sending, tap the address book icon in the address field to pick a saved contact instead of pasting an address.
For Monero wallets, the Wallets tab lists one address per account — the first address in each of that wallet's accounts — rather than every subaddress. The Auto generate subaddresses setting in Privacy settings does not change this. To use a different subaddress, copy it from the Receive screen for that account.

How to customize Cake Wallet in Display settings: pick a light, dark or black OLED theme, an accent color, fiat currency, language, and BTC or sats amounts.
Cake Wallet's Display settings control the app's appearance along with a few handy behavior options — theme, language, fiat currency, and more.

At the top, choose a theme mode:
System — follow your device's light/dark setting
 Light — always light
 Dark — always dark
When a dark mode is active, the picker just below lets you choose between the standard Dark (navy) theme and a Black (OLED) theme that uses true black to save battery on OLED screens.
Selecting the Black theme reveals two extra controls that are hidden for every other theme. Accent color recolors the app's highlights, with a choice of Cake Primary, BCH Green, Bitcoin Yellow, Monero Orange, Tron Red, or Frosting Purple. Below it, the OLED mode switch drives the interface to true black for the deepest contrast and the best battery savings on OLED displays.
